## Practice a capability, not a score

A game should specify what the learner must recall, explain, perform or discuss. Repeated success within its own rules is not sufficient evidence of that capability: assessment must match the intended construct ([Gris and Bengtson, 2021](https://doi.org/10.17083/ijsg.v8i1.383)). Product-specific results for type 1 diabetes (T1D) are collected in the [evidence map](../games/evidence-map.qmd).

**Deliberate practice** means targeted attempts at a specific weakness, with informative feedback and opportunities to revise performance—not simply accumulating play time ([Ericsson et al., 1993](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.100.3.363)). This principle comes from expertise research, not a demonstrated T1D-game effect. Reviews of educational games find learning benefits on average, but effects depend on design and instructional context ([Wouters et al., 2013](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031311); [Clark et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065)).

## What comparative learning research actually supports

The evidence supports investigating games as instructional environments, not replacing every educational format with a game. Wouters et al. synthesised 77 learning comparisons involving 5,547 participants. Games had an average advantage over conventional instruction for learning (standardised mean difference, *d* = 0.29) and retention (*d* = 0.36), whereas the pooled motivation advantage was not statistically significant (*d* = 0.26; 31 comparisons, 2,216 participants). The estimates concern heterogeneous subjects and learners, not newly diagnosed adults with T1D. They also contradict the assumption that a game necessarily motivates better simply because it is a game ([Wouters et al., 2013](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031311)).

Clark et al. distinguished two more useful questions: whether a game outperforms a nongame alternative, and whether a particular design improvement makes the *same game* more effective. Among school-to-undergraduate populations, the first comparison favoured games across 57 studies (Hedges' *g* = 0.33; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19–0.48). Twenty studies comparing enhanced and standard game designs also favoured the enhanced versions (*g* = 0.34; 95% CI 0.17–0.51). These standardised differences describe variation on study-specific assessments; they are not percentage gains in knowledge. Restricting media comparisons to at least moderately credible comparators reduced the average estimate from 0.33 to 0.28. The quality of the alternative matters ([Clark et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065)).

These reviews partly address overlapping literatures and should not be counted as independent replications of one clinical effect. Their moderator analyses are predominantly comparisons between studies, not randomised tests of each design characteristic. For example, an association between group play and larger gains can reflect teacher support, participant selection or different content. The defensible conclusion is that instructional design and delivery affect learning; the evidence does not identify a universal recipe of story, points and social play.

For a T1D project, this changes the comparison worth making. A brochure can provide a concise explanation or remain useful as a reference. A simulation can require predictions and expose consequences of decisions. The relevant question is whether those additional activities improve a specified capability sufficiently to justify their time and complexity. A fair test might compare the same explanation with and without interactive prediction and replay, while retaining equivalent teaching content. This is a **design and evaluation inference**, not a demonstrated superiority of simulation over diabetes education.

## Simulation as hypothesis testing

For a causal-learning simulation, a proposed activity sequence is:

![A proposed learning loop: predict, act, observe, explain, retry and vary.](../../figures/original/predict-act-learning-loop.svg)

Ask for a prediction before revealing the outcome. After the action, show the relevant trajectory and explain the discrepancy. Replay from the same initial state while changing one condition; later vary the starting state as well. Holding other conditions constant makes the comparison interpretable. These are **design inferences**, not evidence that this exact sequence improves T1D outcomes.

Delayed processes require explicit time information. If an action starts now but its effect peaks later, the interface should distinguish action time, ongoing activity and observed consequence. The [physiology chapters](../physiology/index.qmd) describe the relevant delays; the [model chapter](../physiology/model-families.qmd) addresses model validity.

### What the learner should have to infer

A simulation can expose a time course without teaching its cause. Consider a fictional scenario with a planned meal and an action whose effect is delayed. A learner may discover a successful sequence by repeated button presses while retaining the incorrect explanation that the most recent action caused every subsequent change. The proposed remedy is to preserve the decision history, show the prediction beside the observed trajectory, and ask which earlier process remains active. Merely displaying more variables does not resolve the attribution problem.

The following sequence separates exploration from assessment. First, demonstrate a contrast between two otherwise identical scenarios. Second, ask the learner to predict a third scenario before running it. Third, request an explanation in terms of timing or interacting processes. Finally, change the initial conditions and remove the demonstration. The first stages provide instruction; only the last can test whether the learner can reconstruct the relationship without following a visible example. In a deterministic simulation, restarting from the same state supports an interpretable contrast. If variability is part of the model, either control the random realisation during that comparison or explain why repeats differ. These are proposals for experimental control inside the learning task, not claims that human physiology is deterministic.

A useful simulation therefore needs two forms of transparency. **Causal transparency** identifies the relationships represented by its rules. **Boundary transparency** identifies relationships or circumstances it cannot represent. A player should be able to explain both why a simulated result occurred and why that result is not a personal prediction. Increasing physiological detail is justified when it changes the target inference; additional detail that the learner cannot inspect or interpret is not automatically educational value. For coping or communication objectives, an explanatory conversation may be more relevant than any glucose trajectory.

## Feedback that explains the error

Formative feedback provides information the learner can use to improve an attempt. Reviews distinguish task-specific and process-level information from generic praise ([Shute, 2008](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654307313795); [Hattie and Timperley, 2007](https://doi.org/10.3102/003465430298487)).

| Feedback component | Example in a glucose simulation |
|---|---|
| Observed result | Identify when the trajectory diverged from the prediction. |
| Causal explanation | Show which delayed processes overlapped. |
| Model boundary | Identify an omitted or simplified process relevant to this case. |
| Next attempt | Invite a change to one variable and a new prediction. |

This example is a design proposal. Adjacent experimental support comes from two university-student experiments by Butler et al. Participants studied prose passages, answered questions and received feedback; a final test followed two days later. In the first experiment, 60 analysed students received no feedback, the correct answer, or the answer with an explanation. On new inference questions, mean proportions correct were 0.28, 0.30 and 0.45, respectively. Explanation feedback outperformed correct-answer feedback on inference questions, whereas their difference on repeated questions was not statistically significant (0.66 versus 0.62). The second experiment, with 24 analysed students, again favoured explanation feedback for inference ([Butler et al., 2013](https://sites.wustl.edu/mdl1/files/2026/06/Butler-et-al.-2013-Explanation-feedback-is-better-than-correct-answer-feedback-for-promoting-transfer-of-learning.pdf)).

The informative result is the difference between *outcomes*, not simply a positive average effect. An explanation may add little to a test that only asks learners to reproduce the answer already supplied. It can matter when they must apply the relation to a new question. However, these were short laboratory studies of reading and inference, not demonstrations of treatment competence, durable behaviour change or real-life T1D transfer. The clinical application still requires direct evaluation.

Feedback also needs a usable level of specificity. “Incorrect” supplies no corrective model; a complete scientific essay may obscure the decision being corrected. A proposed layered response identifies the result, supplies one relevant explanation and offers optional deeper detail. A correct answer reached for an incorrect reason should prompt an explanation task rather than unqualified praise. Conversely, an unsuccessful outcome does not establish that every decision was wrong: feedback should distinguish the learner's choice, initial constraints and uncertainty in the represented system. This application follows the task- and process-oriented treatment of feedback in [Shute (2008)](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654307313795), rather than treating reward intensity as instructional information.

## Scaffolding and its removal

**Scaffolding** is temporary instructional support: a worked example, prediction choices, a highlighted variable or an explanatory cue. A meta-analysis supports achievement benefits in digital game-based learning, with variation between implementations ([Cai et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09655-0)). It does not identify a universally optimal tutorial length.

A testable progression is to demonstrate one case, guide a second and remove support on a third. Increase complexity by combining previously learned relations, rather than concealing essential information. Assess performance after cues are withdrawn; otherwise the interface may be supplying the reasoning attributed to the learner.

In Clark et al.'s within-game comparisons, enhanced scaffolding covered personalised support, intelligent agents, adaptive experiences and redesigned learning structure. Nine studies contributed 20 effect sizes; the pooled estimate was *g* = 0.41 (95% CI 0.18–0.64). This supports the instructional contribution of additional support as a broad category, not the superiority of any particular hint system. A small subgroup of studies cannot determine the optimal timing or amount of assistance for a newly diagnosed learner ([Clark et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065)).

For implementation, distinguish support for *operating the interface* from support for *solving the learning problem*. Highlighting the pause button removes an interface obstacle. Highlighting the correct action can remove the very reasoning the scenario is meant to practise. Log these separately. A proposed adaptation rule should respond to an interpretable difficulty—such as repeated reversal of the expected time order—not merely to a low score. Provide a route back to a worked explanation, and test the same concept later without the cue. Otherwise successful “adaptive learning” may mean only that the software has learned to give more help.

## Retrieval, variation and transfer

**Retrieval practice** requires recalling or reconstructing an answer before seeing it again. Experiments outside diabetes show that testing can improve delayed retention and, under studied conditions, transfer relative to repeated study ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x); [Butler, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0019902)).

In a T1D game, a prediction, explanation or ordering task can require retrieval without a separate quiz screen. Vary meal timing, context or available information so that memorising one action sequence is insufficient. Space later attempts rather than equating immediate retries with durable retention. These applications remain design hypotheses.

**Transfer** means applying learning to an unpractised task or context. Three complementary probes for causal learning are: predict an unseen trajectory, select an intervention under changed constraints, and explain why the original strategy no longer works. The [evaluation chapter](evaluation.qmd) covers delayed testing, scoring and comparators.

Butler's four experiments are useful for specifying that boundary. Students first studied explanatory passages and then repeatedly studied or answered questions about the material. A final test one week later progressed from repeated questions to new inferences within the original domain and then in a different domain. Repeated testing favoured transfer under these experimental conditions. This was not evidence that any quiz transfers to any practical task; the relationship between trained concepts and new questions was deliberately constructed ([Butler, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0019902)).

In a proposed T1D task, changing the picture of a meal while leaving all quantities and timing unchanged may test recognition under a cosmetic change. Changing the timing, available information and relevant competing process tests a different capability. Neither alone demonstrates use during an unfamiliar real-world situation. Specify the distance between training and assessment rather than calling every new screen “transfer”. A sensible development sequence is to establish retention of the causal relation, then performance in unseen simulated cases, and only then investigate supported application beyond the game.

Repeated failure also needs interpretation. A learner who recognises that their explanation is incomplete may be better calibrated than one who succeeds by guessing but becomes confident. A proposed assessment records both the explanation and confidence before feedback. The objective is not maximum confidence; it is confidence that tracks demonstrated capability and awareness of limitations. This is especially important when a plausible visual model can make a single simulated result appear more certain than its assumptions warrant.

Narrative, shared play and motivation are treated in [game mechanisms](game-mechanisms.qmd); procedure-related distress and psychosocial findings remain in the [evidence map](../games/evidence-map.qmd). Neither simulation nor a glucose model is necessary for every T1D learning objective.
